1: This is a decision briefing for a C I O, a budget officer and an endpoint lead.
An agency weighing a refresh is being asked to fund a distribution point at every field office.
The question is whether that is the right way to deliver content, or whether fewer servers and a better network do the job.
The numbers come from the worked case in the Network and Transport book, a framing pattern with every cost labeled as a planning estimate.
We'll cover the decision, the questions to answer first, the options, the plan, and the ask.
2: The request is about fifty million dollars to refresh distribution point hardware across about fifteen hundred offices.
That's thirty-three thousand dollars per office, nearly twice the cost of a fully loaded server at the program's planning prices.
Configuration Manager's own limits say the estate needs about twenty-four distribution points, not fifteen hundred.
So the position is simple: defer the refresh, pending a network modernization assessment, because the same problem can be solved for about ten million dollars in first-year capital.
The next slide lists what has to be answered before any money moves.
3: Is the fifty million an equipment price or five-year total cost of ownership, and what is bundled beyond the distribution point?
What will the distribution point count be when co-management completes, and in which fiscal year?
What does each office's circuit cost today?
That one number decides whether the alternative pays for itself.
How many managed endpoints are there, since that sets the server count?
And do branch security rules allow devices to share content with each other?
Each answer comes from records the agency already holds.
4: Microsoft's size and scale page sets four thousand clients per distribution point.
Seventy thousand endpoints need eighteen at the ceiling, and twenty-four with headroom.
The other fourteen hundred seventy-six compensate for slow branch circuits, and content has since moved to the cloud.
Microsoft has moved Configuration Manager to an annual release cadence and says new device management work happens in Intune.
Hardware bought this fiscal year depreciates through fiscal 2031, so a refresh can outlive the platform it serves.
The distribution point at every office is.
5: Three options sit on one line.
Refresh keeps fifteen hundred servers, about fifty million dollars, and another capital event every five years, with every server to baseline, scan, patch and carry in the system security plan.
Consolidate puts twenty-four distribution points in twelve hubs for about ten million dollars in first-year capital, which also funds the transport that cloud workloads need.
Retire is the end state: no distribution points at all, once five gates close.
Consolidation is the interim step, so it fits an estate whose management platform is already shrinking.
6: The target uses facilities the agency already has: the primary data center, the recovery site, and ten regional hubs.
Two distribution points per hub gives twenty-four, with capacity for ninety-six thousand clients, which is seventy-three percent used at seventy thousand endpoints.
Regional servers pull from the two data centers, so the fan-out is two to twenty instead of one to fifteen hundred.
Each field office gets a sized internet circuit, a five-G backup for continuity only, and no local server.
The design adds two servers per eight thousand new endpoints.
7: Without a branch server, three mechanisms keep most bytes off the wide area network.
Configuration Manager peer cache lets designated clients share content inside a boundary group.
BranchCache does the same where enabled.
Delivery Optimization peers cloud content, and for hub-and-spoke networks Microsoft recommends Group mode so offices don't all share one address.
All three are optimizations, not dependencies.
Connected Cache is the later step for cloud content.
In the government community cloud the stand-alone form isn't excluded, but it needs its own host and a boundary decision.
Nothing before Phase three depends on it.
8: The twenty-four distribution point tier is interim, not a new floor, and five gates decide when the last one retires.
First, app content: client apps on Intune and nothing still deployed from Configuration Manager.
Second, update content moved, and the old update setting turned off.
Third, imaging moved from task sequences to Windows Autopilot.
Fourth, no Connected Cache running on distribution point hardware.
Fifth, no compliance evidence sourced from the site database.
Close all five in month thirty and retire in month thirty.
Keep the tier rather than force a cutover.
9: First-year capital is about ten million dollars.
Branch equipment is five million, hub equipment about one million, and the control plane and services nearly four million.
Steady-state recurring cost is about fifteen point seven million a year, mostly internet circuits and the security service edge.
Against that, retiring the old circuits at twelve hundred dollars an office a month removes twenty-one point six million, a net saving of about five point nine million a year.
These are planning estimates, not quotes, with hardware at a forty percent discount.
Replace every figure with the estate's own data before a budget submission.
10: Savings ramp as offices move at circuit contract renewal, so year one is a net cost of ten million and the program turns positive in year five, at about three point three million.
The refresh is minus fifty million in year one and recurs at the next cycle, so the five-year difference is about fifty-three million.
One number decides the financial case: current circuit cost per office per month.
Break-even is eight hundred seventy-three dollars.
Above it, the program funds itself.
Below it, it's still cheaper than the refresh, but justify it on capability and mission.
11: Phase zero, the first six months, costs about one point eight million.
It covers design, the security accreditation package, the control plane, and a ten-site pilot, and it exits on authorization, thirty stable days, and validated costs.
Phase one builds the twelve hubs and the twenty-four distribution points.
Phase two moves offices in waves, timed to circuit renewals so each wave helps fund the next, and no old circuit retires until its replacement telemetry is confirmed.
Phase three adds Microsoft 365 optimization and caching, and retires servers only as the gates close.
Accreditation, not procurement, is the critical path.
12: The implementation runs in ten stages, in order, and every stage cites Microsoft Learn.
Stage one analyzes the existing estate: list every distribution point, its boundary groups and the clients it serves, and pull circuit cost and quality for each office.
Stage two sizes the result against Microsoft's limits.
Stage three is the funding gate, the exit from Phase zero, where leadership funds the hub tier or stops.
Stage four builds the hubs with pull distribution points, groups and prestaged content.
Stage five turns on peer caching.
The implementation guide and the scripts kit are linked on the slide.
13: Stage six moves offices in waves at circuit renewal: each office's boundary joins its hub's boundary group, then the office server goes read-only and retires.
Stage seven packages applications once with P S App Deploy Toolkit, so Configuration Manager and Intune behave the same.
Stage eight shifts co-management workloads to Intune, starting with apps and updates.
Stage nine adds Connected Cache at the hubs for cloud content.
Stage ten closes the five gates, and only then retires the last distribution point.
The guide and the scripts kit are linked here too, for the people who will do the work.
14: Accreditation slips: start the package in Phase zero, and a twelve-month slip still leaves the case better than the refresh, by about forty-seven million, though break-even moves past year five.
Circuit cost comes in below the assumption: validate it before submission.
And replacement telemetry lags a cutover: begin coordination in Phase zero and gate each office on it.
Ten assumptions in all are ordered by impact.
Check circuit cost, endpoint count and terrestrial availability first.
The architectural conclusion holds across the range; the financial one depends on the circuit number.
15: There's a follow-on that makes consolidation safer: standard application packaging.
Intune Win32 apps must install silently, and Gate one only closes when the app catalog moves, not just a setting.
If each app is packaged twice, the two paths behave differently.

P S App Deploy Toolkit is a PowerShell framework that standardizes deployment to Windows at scale, with first-class support for Intune and Configuration Manager, and phases for before, during and after the install.
That's program design guidance, and it follows the decision rather than conditioning it.
16: Defer the fifty million dollar refresh pending a network modernization assessment.
Have the sponsor state whether it is acquisition or five-year cost, and itemize the scope.
Validate the ten assumptions, starting with circuit cost and endpoint count.
Fund Phase zero, about one point eight million over six months.
Track the five gates, not a date, for the last server.
The owner is the sponsor with the C I O, and the timing is before refresh money is committed.
The decision guide and the project plan carry the detail, and both are linked on this slide.
